**What it does:** Serpzilla is a self-serve marketplace of publisher sites. You browse sites, filter by metrics, niche, language and price, and buy one of three things:
- **Guest posts**: a new article on the publisher's site, with your link.
- **Link insertions**: your link added to an existing page.
- **Rented links**: a link you pay for monthly, which disappears if you stop paying.

It also has an MCP server, so you can drive it from an agent. You choose each site and see its price yourself. Nobody does outreach for you.

**What these are:** They're paid links. Google's spam policy treats buying links that pass ranking credit as link spam. That's the whole purpose of most marketplace placements, so the risk comes with the product. Paid links are only within the rules if they carry `rel="sponsored"` or `nofollow`. A sponsored link mostly won't help rankings, so you'd be paying mainly for AI citations and referral traffic.

The three formats carry different risk:
- **Rented links** are the most footprint-heavy. They're sitewide or recurring, easy to spot, and they vanish when you stop paying.
- **Insertions into old articles** are "niche edits", which the guidance says to avoid.
- **Guest posts** on real editorial sites are the most defensible. Keep the anchors branded or plain, not keyword-rich.

**Is it worth it?** It depends on what you want.
- **If you want rankings from followed links:** I wouldn't recommend it. You'd be paying for something Google calls manipulation, on sites that sell links to anyone and so tend to be weak signals. A manual action or a quiet devaluation can cost more than the links ever earned.
- **If you want AI citations or referral traffic:** it can work in a limited way. Pick sites that are already cited for your category's prompts, require a sponsored or nofollow attribute and a disclosure, and treat it as advertising spend.

**If you try it anyway:**
- Vet each site yourself. Check that its traffic is real and not collapsing, that it's topically relevant, and that its outbound links aren't mostly unrelated commercial anchors.
- Start with a few guest posts, not a bulk order. Spread them across several pages and avoid pointing everything at one commercial page.
- Don't let a marketplace's own metrics (DR or similar) stand in for that vetting.

**Cheaper and safer first:**
- Reclaim unlinked mentions.
- Get listed on partner and integration pages.
- Get into "best X" lists.
- Use data-led PR.
- Add internal links to the pages you want to rank.

Alternatives in the same category are Collaborator, WhitePress and Adsy (also marketplaces), or LinkDR if you'd rather pay for a managed service than pick sites yourself.

I haven't verified current Serpzilla pricing, catalog quality or terms. Check those on their site before spending anything.

**What it does**

Serpzilla is a self-serve marketplace of publisher sites. You browse sites, check their metrics and prices, and buy one of three things:
- **Guest posts**, where a new article is published on the site with a link to you.
- **Link insertions**, where a link is added to an existing page (often called "niche edits").
- **Monthly rented links**, which stay up only while you keep paying.

It also has an MCP server, so you can drive it from an agent. I'm working from my reference notes and haven't checked the current catalog or pricing, so verify those on their site.

**Is it worth it?**

The main risk is Google's spam policy. Buying links that pass ranking credit is link spam, and the marketplace model is built around exactly that. Paid placements are only safe if they carry `rel="sponsored"` or `rel="nofollow"`. Most buyers want followed links, which is where the penalty risk comes from.

The three products carry different amounts of risk:
- **Insertions into old articles** are the riskiest. Avoid them.
- **Rented links** are a poor deal. The link disappears when you stop paying, and a pattern of them is easy for Google to spot.
- **Guest posts on real editorial sites** are the least risky. Use branded or plain anchors, not keyword-rich ones.

Placements can still pay off in two ways, and both work even with a nofollow or sponsored link:
- They can get you mentioned on pages AI engines already cite.
- They can send referral traffic.

**If you try it**
1. Check first that links are actually your bottleneck. Compare referring domains for your page against the pages that outrank it. If the gap is content or intent, links won't fix it.
2. Vet each site before buying. Look for organic traffic that isn't falling, topical relevance, and real editorial standards. Skip sites whose outbound links are mostly unrelated commercial anchors, and sites that obviously sell links to anyone.
3. Spread links across several pages, with mostly branded anchors.
4. Start with a small test, a few placements, and watch rankings and AI mentions over 1–3 months.

**Cheaper options to try first**
- Reclaiming unlinked mentions of your brand.
- Partner, integration and customer pages.
- Getting included in "best X" lists.
- Digital PR.
- Directory listings.

If you want it done for you, LinkDR is a managed placement service. Collaborator, WhitePress and Adsy are marketplaces similar to Serpzilla. Those are also paid links, so the same rules apply.

## Where the first 20 come from

| Source | Realistic yield | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **Directories and launch sites** (Product Hunt, AlternativeTo, SaaS and AI directories, relevant awesome-lists) | 6-8 | A few hours |
| **Your own footprint** (founder LinkedIn, GitHub, X, Crunchbase, any other profile you control, plus partner, customer, vendor and integration pages) | 4-6 | Low |
| **Unlinked mentions** (set up Google Alerts for your brand and founder names, then email the author and ask for the link) | 1-3 | Low |
| **"Best X" list inclusion** (find listicles in your category and ask for an honest evaluation) | 2-4 | Medium |
| **One linkable asset** (a free tool, template, glossary or small data study) | 2-4 over time | Highest, but it compounds |
| **Expert quotes and podcasts** (answer journalist requests, guest on small podcasts) | 1-3 | Medium |

Directories only lay the foundation. They won't move rankings much, but they get you to 8-10 links quickly. The "best X" lists and the asset are what actually help rankings and AI citations.

## Order of work

1. **Week 1:** Fill in every profile you control and submit to directories. Email any customers, partners and integration vendors and ask for a link. Set up Google Alerts.
2. **Week 2:** Run the free searches below to build a list of 20-30 "best X" and resource pages. Add internal links from your strongest pages to the pages you want to rank.
3. **Weeks 3-4:** Send short, personalized outreach to the best 10-15 prospects. Start on one linkable asset.
4. **Ongoing:** Answer journalist requests and give your asset to the resource-page owners.

# First 20 backlinks on a $0 budget

With no budget, skip the paid placement services (LinkDR, Serpzilla and similar). They're paid links, so they'd need `rel="sponsored"` anyway. Free tactics will get you to 20 if you work them in order of effort and yield.

## Tier 1: Links you can get this week (aim for 8–10)

1. **Your own footprint.** Link your site from every profile you control: founder and team LinkedIn, X, GitHub, Crunchbase, personal sites, and the Slack, Discord and community profiles you already have. Many of these are nofollow, but they establish the foundation and help AI engines recognize the brand.
2. **Directories and launch sites.** Submit to Product Hunt, AlternativeTo, relevant startup and SaaS directories, and awesome-lists on GitHub for your category. These are free and low-quality individually, but they're easy foundation links. The directory-submissions skill has a tracker if you want one.
3. **Partners, customers and vendors.** Ask every tool you integrate with, every customer who'd say yes, and every vendor you use for a listing on their partner page, integrations marketplace, case study or "built with" page. These are relevant and usually high quality.
4. **Unlinked mentions.** Set up Google Alerts for your brand and founder names, and search `"yourbrand" -site:yourdomain.com`. Anyone who already wrote about you gets a short "could you link to us?" email.

## Tier 2: Outreach that takes effort (aim for 6–8)

5. **"Best X" list inclusion.** Search `best [your category]`, `[category] alternatives` and `intitle:"best" [category]`. Pitch the authors of the lists that rank. These pages are also what AI engines cite, so a mention helps even without a link. Ask for an honest evaluation, and offer a free account or demo access. If you give free access in exchange for a review, the link should carry a nofollow or sponsored attribute.
6. **Resource and tools pages.** Use `inurl:resources` or `intitle:"tools"` plus your niche to find curated lists, then pitch a one-line addition.
7. **Broken-link replacement.** Find dead links on pages in your niche and offer your content as the replacement. This only works if you have a relevant page to offer.
8. **Journalist and expert requests.** Respond to free requests on Qwoted and Featured, and on X or LinkedIn via #journorequest. Founders with real expertise land editorial links this way for $0.

## Tier 3: Build one asset (aim for 3–5)

9. **Create one thing worth citing.** The best options are original data from your own users or a small survey, a free calculator, a template, or a glossary of your category's terms. Link it internally to the page you most want to rank.
10. **Share it where practitioners hang out.** Participate in Reddit, Hacker News and niche communities as yourself, and don't drop links cold. Podcast guesting is also free and often produces a link from the show notes.

## Rules to stay safe

- Don't swap links in bulk, use networks or automated tools, or accept "niche edit" offers. Those will show up in your inbox as soon as you start outreach.
- Let the other site pick the anchor text. Don't ask for keyword-rich anchors.
- Spread links across pages, not only the homepage.
- Before you start outreach, add internal links from your strongest pages to the page you want to rank. It costs nothing.

## Realistic expectations

With about 5 hours a week, Tier 1 gets you 8–10 links in the first 2–3 weeks. Reaching 20 takes 6–8 weeks once outreach replies start coming in. Expect a 10–20% reply rate on well-targeted, personalized emails.

**1. Check what you already have (about 2 hours, 0–3 links)**

- Ask customers, integration partners and tools you use whether they have a partners or case-study page.

**4. Expert contributions (about 3–5 links)**
- Respond to journalist requests through free channels, including Qwoted, Featured, and the free tiers of similar services.
- Pitch podcasts in your niche, since show notes usually link to guests.
- Offer a guest article to editorial sites only. Skip any "write for us" networks.

**5. One linkable asset (long-term)**
Build one thing people will cite, such as a small free tool, a template, or original data from your own users. Everything else works better when you have something worth linking to.

- Spread links across the pages that need them, not just the homepage.

**Usually no.** Google has said for years that it ignores most spammy links automatically, and Semrush's "toxic score" is its own heuristic, not a Google signal. Disavowing everything it flags rarely helps and can hurt if you disavow links that were actually helping.

**Don't disavow if:**
- The links are just low-quality scrapers, directories, or random spam. This is normal noise and Google discounts it.
- You have no manual action and no unexplained ranking or traffic drop.
- The only evidence is the Semrush score.

**Disavow if:**
